chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, that he said:

"I was with 'Isa ibn Musa when a thief was brought, and with him was a man from the family of 'Umar. He began questioning me, so I said: What do you say about the thief when he confesses against himself that he stole? He said: His hand is cut off. I said: Then what do you say about the fornicator when he confesses against himself four times? He said: We stone him. I said: Then what prevents you, in the case of the thief, if he confesses against himself twice, from cutting him off, so that he would be in the position of the fornicator?"

key_terms.أَرْبَعَ مَرَّاتٍ: four times; the number of confessions mentioned for zina
key_terms.أَقَرَّ: he confessed; acknowledged guilt against himself
key_terms.اَلزَّانِي: the fornicator; the person guilty of zina
key_terms.اَلسَّارِقِ: the thief; the person accused or confessing to theft
key_terms.مَرَّتَيْنِ: twice; the number of confessions being argued for theft
key_terms.نَرْجُمُهُ: we stone him; the hadd punishment stated here for zina
key_terms.يُقْطَعُ: his hand is cut off; the hadd punishment for theft

ai.seo_question: How many times must a thief confess before the hadd punishment is carried out in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses judicial reasoning concerning the hadd punishment for theft in comparison with zina. It presents an argument based on analogy between the number of confessions considered sufficient for establishing legal punishment in different crimes, highlighting debate in legal procedure and evidentiary standards.
